meta.description: UK EPC and MEES regulatory timeline data — totem.systems
meta.notes: Proposed dates use 1 Jan / 1 Apr of target year as placeholder. Always verify against latest DESNZ / MHCLG publications.

milestones.title: EPCs Mandatory on Sale & Let
milestones.summary: Energy Performance Certificates became mandatory for all properties marketed for sale or rent across England, Wales and Scotland. The familiar A–G rating scale was introduced under the EU Energy Performance of Buildings Directive.
milestones.detail:
The EU Energy Performance of Buildings Directive (EPBD 2002/91/EC) required all member states to introduce EPCs. In England and Wales this was implemented through the Energy Performance of Buildings (Certificates and Inspections) Regulations 2007, with phased introduction from August 2007 through to October 2008.

EPCs must be commissioned before a property is marketed for rent or sale. Certificates are valid for 10 years. A new EPC is only required when the existing one expires or when material changes are made to the property.

For PBSA operators, a valid EPC must be available at the point of marketing each unit. New-build PBSA schemes require an EPC before occupation. Whether a building is assessed under the domestic or non-domestic EPC methodology depends on configuration — purpose-built blocks with communal facilities are typically rated non-domestically.
milestones.totemAngle: Totem's live energy monitoring gives PBSA operators real-time visibility of actual energy use — providing the evidence base to challenge or improve EPC ratings and demonstrate performance between assessments.
milestones.source: Energy Performance of Buildings (Certificates and Inspections) Regulations 2007

milestones.title: MEES Phase 1 — Residential EPC E (New & Renewed Tenancies)
milestones.summary: Minimum EPC E required for all new or renewed residential tenancies in England and Wales. Properties rated F or G could not be legally let without a registered exemption. Fines up to £4,000 per property.
milestones.detail:
The Domestic Minimum Energy Efficiency Standard (MEES) Regulations came into force on 1 April 2018. Landlords of F or G rated properties could not grant new or renewed tenancies without either improving the property to EPC E or registering an exemption on the national PRS Exemptions Register.

Exemptions are available where:
• All relevant energy efficiency improvements have been made and the property still cannot reach EPC E
• The cost of required improvements would exceed £3,500 net of any available third-party funding
• A qualified assessor confirms no cost-effective improvements exist
• The property is listed or in a conservation area and consent for works has been refused
• Tenant consent has been withheld (5-year exemption)

PBSA and HMO properties assessed under the domestic EPC framework — typically smaller HMOs and some converted buildings — are subject to these requirements. Many PBSA assets built before 2005 carried F or G ratings and required remedial heating, insulation or glazing works before re-letting.
milestones.totemAngle: Real-time energy monitoring from Totem enables PBSA operators to evidence energy performance improvements between EPC assessments — providing continuous data rather than a single-point snapshot.
milestones.source: Energy Efficiency (Private Rented Property)(England and Wales) Regulations 2015

milestones.title: Non-Domestic MEES Phase 1 — Commercial EPC E (New Leases)
milestones.summary: EPC E became the minimum for new or renewed non-domestic (commercial) leases in England and Wales. Applies to most purpose-built student accommodation assessed under the non-domestic EPC framework. Fines up to £150,000.
milestones.detail:
The Non-Domestic MEES Regulations mirrored the residential changes but for commercial property. From 1 April 2018, it became unlawful to grant a new or renewed lease on premises rated F or G.

For PBSA operators, whether a building is assessed under the domestic or non-domestic EPC methodology is determined by configuration:
• Purpose-built blocks of six or more storeys, or blocks with centralised mechanical ventilation / communal HVAC, are typically rated non-domestically (using SBEM methodology)
• Smaller converted HMOs and en-suite cluster blocks may be rated domestically (SAP methodology)

Non-domestic EPC F or G = unlawful to let from April 2018. Maximum penalties: up to £150,000 per property (calculated daily based on rateable value). Exemptions broadly mirror the residential regime but are administered differently.
milestones.totemAngle: Totem integrates with BMS and building management systems to deliver the granular energy data PBSA operators need to justify EPC improvement programmes and validate retrofit outcomes.
milestones.source: Energy Efficiency (Private Rented Property)(England and Wales) Regulations 2015

milestones.title: MEES Phase 2 — Residential EPC E (All Existing Tenancies)
milestones.summary: The EPC E minimum was extended to ALL existing residential tenancies — not just new ones. Landlords with ongoing tenancies on F or G rated properties were required to improve or register an exemption. Enforcement powers passed to local authorities.
milestones.detail:
From 1 April 2020, it became unlawful for a landlord to continue letting any residential property rated F or G — regardless of when the tenancy was originally granted — without a valid exemption on the PRS Exemptions Register.

Key enforcement details:
• Enforcement authority: local housing authorities (LHAs)
• Penalty notices can be issued up to 18 months after a breach
• Maximum fine: £4,000 per property per breach
• Publication of enforcement notices in a public register

The cost cap for required improvements remained at £3,500 net of third-party funding (e.g. ECO scheme grants, local authority funding). If a property cannot be improved to EPC E within this cap, a 'cost cap exemption' can be registered for five years, after which it must be reviewed.

For PBSA operators, this extension created immediate compliance risk for any in-tenancy assets still rated F or G. Many operators used the 2018–2020 window to commission improvement works across their portfolios.
milestones.totemAngle: Totem monitors energy consumption across entire PBSA portfolios in real time — flagging underperforming buildings before they become compliance liabilities and helping operators prioritise retrofit spend.
milestones.source: Energy Efficiency (Private Rented Property)(England and Wales) Regulations 2015 (amended)

milestones.title: Non-Domestic MEES Phase 2 — Commercial EPC E (All Leases)
milestones.summary: EPC E extended to ALL existing non-domestic leases — including tenancies already in progress. PBSA assets rated under the commercial EPC framework must now be EPC E or above to be legally let. Maximum fines: £150,000 per property.
milestones.detail:
The most significant commercial MEES change to date. From 1 April 2023, landlords cannot lawfully continue to let commercial premises rated F or G regardless of when the tenancy was granted — bringing commercial MEES in line with the residential extension of 2020.

Enforcement is by local weights and measures authorities (trading standards officers). Financial penalties are calculated on a sliding scale based on rateable value and length of breach, capped at £150,000 per property. Enforcement actions are published in the publicly accessible MEES enforcement register.

For PBSA operators with large portfolios of older non-domestic rated stock, April 2023 created significant retrofit pressure — particularly for blocks built in the 1990s and 2000s that had not been upgraded since the MEES phase 1 deadline in 2018.
milestones.totemAngle: Totem's energy monitoring has helped PBSA operators identify and prioritise buildings at risk of non-compliance before critical deadlines — and provide measurable evidence of retrofit outcomes to EPC assessors.
milestones.source: Energy Efficiency (Private Rented Property)(England and Wales) Regulations 2015 (amended 2019)

milestones.title: Renters' Rights Act 2025 — In Force
milestones.summary: The Renters' Rights Act 2025 came into force on 1 May 2026, abolishing Section 21 'no fault' evictions and applying the new Decent Homes Standard to the private rented sector for the first time. Energy efficiency requirements (MEES) are now embedded as a criterion of the DHS, creating dual compliance obligations for landlords.
milestones.detail:
The Renters' Rights Act 2025 received Royal Assent and its key provisions took effect on 1 May 2026. Core changes:

• Section 21 'no fault' evictions abolished: landlords may only terminate tenancies using specified grounds under Section 8
• Decent Homes Standard (DHS) extended to the private rented sector for the first time — properties must now meet the DHS, which includes energy efficiency and thermal comfort criteria
• A new Private Rented Sector Database is being established, requiring landlords to register their properties
• MEES requirements form criterion D of the new DHS, meaning EPC compliance obligations are now embedded in broader fitness standards — a below-minimum EPC triggers both a MEES breach and a DHS non-compliance
• Landlords with tenancies created before 1 May 2026 were required to provide tenants with a statutory Information Sheet by 31 May 2026 (fines up to £7,000 for non-compliance)

For PBSA operators, the Act reinforces the link between energy efficiency and legal compliance. A property below the required EPC standard no longer only breaches MEES but also triggers DHS non-compliance, creating dual enforcement risk from both local housing authorities and trading standards.
milestones.totemAngle: The Act embeds energy performance into the core legal standard for private rental — Totem's live monitoring helps PBSA operators maintain continuous DHS compliance evidence and flag buildings at risk of falling below EPC thresholds before enforcement action is triggered.
milestones.source: Renters' Rights Act 2025 / MHCLG Renters' Rights Act Information Sheet 2026 (published 20 March 2026)

milestones.title: EPC Methodology Reform — Home Energy Model (HEM)
milestones.summary: The UK Government is replacing the SAP-based EPC methodology with the new Home Energy Model (HEM), introducing four headline metrics: fabric performance, heating system, smart readiness, and energy cost. A partial government response was published in January 2026; the HEM:EPC methodology consultation ran January–March 2026 and closed on 18 March 2026. Government is currently analysing responses — a full response is expected later in 2026. Full implementation expected second half of 2027.
milestones.detail:
The reformed EPC framework replaces SAP (Standard Assessment Procedure) with the Home Energy Model (HEM). Key developments in 2025–2026:

• January 2026: MHCLG/DESNZ published a partial government response to the EPB Reforms consultation, confirming the direction of EPC reform and some implementation details.
• January–March 2026: A further consultation ran on HEM:EPC methodology — specifically how each of the four new metrics will be calculated and banded on the new-style certificate. This consultation closed on 18 March 2026 and government is analysing responses. A full government response is expected later in 2026.
• Following engagement with industry on the delivery timeline, government has moved the launch of the reforms to the second half of 2027 (delayed from the earlier October 2026 target).

The four new headline EPC metrics are:
1. Fabric Performance — insulation and building fabric quality
2. Heating System — efficiency and carbon intensity of the installed heat source
3. Smart Readiness — ability to respond to grid signals and optimise consumption
4. Energy Cost — estimated running costs for occupants

For non-domestic buildings (including many PBSA assets assessed under SBEM), the existing headline metric will be retained for now. Updates to the National Calculation Methodology for non-domestic buildings are expected, but the non-domestic transition timeline has not yet been confirmed. Outstanding questions on how non-domestic HEM methodology will apply to PBSA remain subject to further DESNZ guidance.
milestones.totemAngle: Totem's metered consumption data becomes even more valuable under the new HEM framework that weights actual energy use, heating system performance, and smart readiness — real-time monitoring data directly supports favourable assessments under the new metrics.
milestones.source: MHCLG/DESNZ: Reforms to the Energy Performance of Buildings Regime — Partial Government Response (January 2026); HEM:EPC Methodology Consultation (closed 18 March 2026, response pending)

milestones.title: Scotland: Heat in Buildings Bill — Draft Published
milestones.summary: Scotland's draft Buildings (Heating and Energy Performance) and Heat Networks (Scotland) Bill was published in November 2025. The Bill was not introduced during Session 6 (parliament dissolved May 2026). Introduction to Parliament is now expected in Session 7 of the new Scottish Parliament, as early as possible following the May 2026 election.
milestones.detail:
The Scottish Government published the draft Buildings (Heating and Energy Performance) and Heat Networks (Scotland) Bill on 18 November 2025, following the Cabinet Secretary for Housing's statement to Parliament. The Bill was not introduced to the Session 6 parliament before the May 2026 election. Key provisions of the draft Bill:

• All buildings must have zero direct emissions heating systems by 2045
• Fossil fuel heating systems (gas boilers, oil boilers) will become non-compliant on a statutory timeline
• The Bill also provides the legislative framework for heat network licensing and installation standards
• Introduction to Parliament in Session 7 (new parliament) is intended as early as possible, subject to the outcome of the May 2026 Scottish Parliament election

Separately, the Scottish Government consulted between June–August 2025 on draft Energy Efficiency (Domestic Private Rented Property) (Scotland) Regulations, proposing:
• EPC Heat Retention Rating Band C required for new lets from 2028
• All lets from 2033

Scotland is also rolling out new-style EPC regulations (with a redesigned certificate) planned to come into force in October 2026, ahead of the England and Wales HEM reform.

For Scottish PBSA operators, the direction is clear and more demanding than the MEES framework south of the border. Fossil fuel heating in Scottish student accommodation will become non-compliant on a fixed statutory timeline.
milestones.totemAngle: Totem works with PBSA operators in Scotland to model the performance of existing heating systems and build the evidence base for compliant low-carbon upgrade programmes — from initial assessment through to post-installation verification.
milestones.source: Scottish Government: Draft Buildings (Heating and Energy Performance) and Heat Networks (Scotland) Bill, November 2025

milestones.title: Proposed: Scotland PRS MEES — EPC Heat Retention Band C (New Lets)
milestones.summary: Scotland is consulting on requiring all new private rented sector tenancies to meet EPC Heat Retention Rating Band C from 2028, with all tenancies required to comply by 2033. Separate from and running in parallel with the England and Wales MEES EPC C proposals.
milestones.detail:
The Scottish Government consulted (June–August 2025) on draft Energy Efficiency (Domestic Private Rented Property) (Scotland) Regulations under existing powers, independent of the Heat in Buildings Bill. Key proposals:

• New lets: EPC Heat Retention Rating Band C from 2028
• All existing lets: compliance required by 2033

Important distinctions from England and Wales MEES:
• Scotland uses a separate EPC methodology that is also being reformed — new EPC regulations planned for October 2026 introduce a redesigned certificate
• The 'Heat Retention Rating' metric may differ from the fabric or overall EPC rating used in England and Wales MEES
• Enforcement and exemption frameworks are set separately by Scottish Ministers

For PBSA operators with Scottish assets, this creates a distinct compliance obligation running alongside (and in some respects ahead of) the England and Wales timeline. The 2033 all-lets date is more generous than England's proposed 2030 date, but the Heat in Buildings Bill requirements on heating systems decarbonisation are significantly more demanding.
milestones.totemAngle: Totem's live energy monitoring provides the portfolio-level performance data Scottish PBSA operators need to identify which buildings require intervention under the new Heat Retention Rating standard, and to demonstrate progress to regulators.
milestones.source: Scottish Government: Draft Energy Efficiency (Domestic Private Rented Property) (Scotland) Regulations — Consultation, June 2025

milestones.title: Proposed: Residential EPC C — New & Renewed Tenancies (England & Wales)
milestones.summary: The Government's response to the PRS MEES consultation (published May 2026) confirms EPC C will be required for all new or renewed residential tenancies in England and Wales from 2028. Landlord spending cap confirmed at £10,000 per property. Subject to a statutory instrument expected to come into force in 2027.
milestones.detail:
The Government published its response to the 'Improving the Energy Performance of Privately Rented Homes' consultation in May 2026. Key confirmed decisions:

• 2028: EPC C required for new or renewed tenancies in England and Wales
• 2030 (1 October): EPC C required for all existing tenancies
• Landlord spending cap: £10,000 per property (net of available grants), with a 10-year exemption validity if the standard cannot be achieved within this cap
• A statutory instrument to update the PRS Regulations is expected to come into force in 2027
• Properties achieving EPC C under the current methodology before new HEM-based EPCs are introduced will be treated as compliant until that EPC expires

The confirmed £10,000 cost cap replaces the earlier consultation proposal of £15,000. The government also confirmed a 'dual-metric standard' approach — compliance under the new framework will require meeting a fabric performance standard, followed by landlord discretion to meet either a heating system standard or a smart readiness standard.

For PBSA operators, this is the most operationally significant deadline approaching. Properties currently rated D (common in PBSA built 2000–2015) will require improvement by 2028 for any new or renewed tenancies. Early EPC audits and retrofit planning should already be underway.
milestones.totemAngle: Totem helps PBSA operators build the evidence base for EPC C upgrade programmes — identifying the highest-impact interventions through live energy data, anomaly detection and building performance benchmarking.
milestones.source: MHCLG: Improving the Energy Performance of Privately Rented Homes — Government Response (May 2026)

milestones.title: Proposed: Non-Domestic MEES C
milestones.summary: Proposals to raise the non-domestic (commercial) MEES minimum to EPC C by 2027–2028. Would apply to PBSA assets assessed under the commercial EPC framework. Status: proposed under previous government, current Labour position under review.
milestones.detail:
The previous Conservative Government consulted on a stepped trajectory for non-domestic MEES:
• EPC C by 2027
• EPC B by 2030

This trajectory was never legislated and has not been formally confirmed or rejected by the Labour Government. Non-domestic MEES reform is referenced in ongoing DESNZ policy workstreams. In January 2026, government confirmed it will retain the existing headline non-domestic EPC metric for now, with updates to requirements expected — a full government response on remaining non-domestic questions is anticipated in 2026.

For non-domestically rated PBSA, an EPC C requirement would be particularly challenging because:
• Non-domestic EPCs use SBEM methodology, which differs from domestic SAP — the gap between E and C can be substantial
• Many PBSA blocks built in the 1990s–2000s are rated D or E under this framework
• Achieving EPC C under SBEM typically requires significant HVAC, controls, lighting and fabric improvements

Operators with non-domestically rated PBSA stock should not assume this trajectory has been abandoned. Planning on the basis that a C minimum is coming — even if the precise date shifts — is prudent.
milestones.totemAngle: Totem's BMS integration and live energy analytics give PBSA operators the performance data needed to model EPC trajectories, assess improvement options and prioritise capital expenditure across their portfolios.

milestones.title: Proposed: Residential EPC C — All Existing Tenancies (England & Wales)
milestones.summary: All existing residential tenancies in England and Wales must meet EPC C by 1 October 2030 — the single compliance date confirmed in the May 2026 government response. Landlord spending cap confirmed at £10,000. Subject to a statutory instrument expected in 2027.
milestones.detail:
The Government's May 2026 response to the PRS MEES consultation confirmed 1 October 2030 as the single compliance date for all existing residential tenancies to meet EPC C in England and Wales.

Key confirmed details:
• Single compliance date: 1 October 2030 (all tenancies, regardless of when granted)
• Landlord spending cap: £10,000 per property (10-year exemption if standard unachievable within this cap)
• The statutory instrument enabling updated PRS Regulations is expected to come into force in 2027
• Properties already compliant under existing EPC methodology will be treated as compliant until that EPC expires

Scale of challenge for PBSA operators:
• Properties rated D (common in pre-2015 PBSA) require meaningful improvement works — EPC D to C is a significant step
• Properties rated E face more substantial and costly retrofit programmes
• With approximately 4 years to the 2030 deadline and SI legislation anticipated in 2027, operators need retrofit roadmaps and capital plans in place now

The 2030 deadline effectively makes EPC C the new minimum operating standard for all privately rented residential property in England and Wales. PBSA operators should be commissioning EPC audits across their entire portfolio and contracting energy monitoring to evidence actual performance before and after retrofit works.
milestones.totemAngle: Totem provides portfolio-level energy monitoring enabling PBSA operators to identify which buildings carry the highest EPC risk, track retrofit outcomes against predicted EPC uplift, and evidence compliance to investors and local authorities.
milestones.source: MHCLG: Improving the Energy Performance of Privately Rented Homes — Government Response (May 2026)

milestones.title: Proposed: Social Rented Sector MEES — EPC C by 2030 (England)
milestones.summary: The Government's response to the social rented homes energy efficiency consultation (published 1 April 2026) confirmed that all social rented homes in England must meet EPC C or equivalent by 1 April 2030 — the first statutory minimum EPC standard for the social rented sector. A second-metric compliance requirement follows by 2039. Subject to a statutory instrument.
milestones.detail:
MHCLG published the government response to 'Improving the Energy Efficiency of Socially Rented Homes in England' on 1 April 2026. Key confirmed decisions:

• Phase 1 (by 1 April 2030): Social housing providers must ensure all social rented properties meet EPC C or equivalent against any ONE of: fabric performance, smart readiness, or heating system (under reformed EPC metrics), or have a valid exemption registered
• Phase 2 (by 1 April 2039): Properties must also meet EPC C against a SECOND EPC metric from the same set
• Spending exemption: Providers may register an exemption if the standard cannot be achieved within the applicable spend threshold (at least £10,000 for the second-metric exemption)
• A statutory instrument is required to give these requirements legal force

Social rented homes are currently not subject to any statutory MEES standard — this represents an entirely new compliance obligation for housing associations and local authority landlords. The 2030 deadline aligns with the private rented sector EPC C deadline.

For PBSA operators who manage accommodation under nomination agreements or partnership arrangements with social landlords, this framework may create indirect compliance considerations. The dual-metric approach mirrors the PRS MEES framework and is designed to align with the reformed HEM-based EPC regime expected in 2027.
milestones.totemAngle: PBSA operators providing accommodation under nomination agreements or partnerships with social landlords should note this new compliance obligation — Totem's portfolio energy monitoring provides the evidence base to demonstrate EPC performance across mixed-tenure and mixed-landlord stock.
milestones.source: MHCLG: Improving the Energy Efficiency of Socially Rented Homes in England — Government Response (1 April 2026)

milestones.title: Proposed: Non-Domestic MEES B
milestones.summary: Long-standing proposals to raise the non-domestic (commercial) MEES minimum to EPC B by 2030. Would represent the most demanding energy standard ever required for commercial property in the UK. Status: proposed, not yet legislated.
milestones.detail:
An EPC B minimum for commercial property by 2030 was proposed under the previous Conservative Government as part of a stepped non-domestic trajectory. It has not been formally withdrawn by Labour, though no legislation has followed.

Achieving EPC B under the non-domestic framework (SBEM) is highly demanding for older stock. It typically requires:
• Near-Passivhaus-equivalent fabric performance
• Low-carbon heating systems (heat pumps, heat networks)
• Advanced building controls and BMS
• High-efficiency ventilation with heat recovery
• Significant on-site renewable generation

For PBSA operators, EPC B by 2030 (if legislated) would require deep retrofit of almost all pre-2010 stock — with an exemption route for economically unviable buildings.

This target is widely regarded as aspirational and the most likely element of the non-domestic trajectory to be delayed or revised. However, the direction of travel is unambiguous: energy standards for commercial property will continue to tighten.
milestones.totemAngle: Totem's continuous monitoring platform provides the performance data needed to demonstrate EPC B-equivalent operation and identify the precise energy gap between current and target performance — building the business case for investment.

milestones.title: Conservative EPC C Target for New Tenancies by 2025 — Dropped
milestones.summary: The 2021 Conservative Government consultation proposed requiring EPC C for new residential tenancies by 2025 and all tenancies by 2028. This target was abandoned by Rishi Sunak in September 2023. Superseded by Labour's revised 2028/2030 targets.
milestones.detail:
The 2021 BEIS consultation 'Improving the energy performance of privately rented homes' proposed:
• EPC C required for new tenancies: from 2025
• EPC C required for all tenancies: from 2028
• Landlord spending cap: £10,000 per property

In September 2023, Prime Minister Rishi Sunak announced that the 2025 target would not proceed, citing the cost burden on landlords during the cost-of-living crisis. The announcement also removed several other green commitments, including boiler upgrade timelines.

The decision was welcomed by landlord associations (NRLA, ARLA) but criticised by environmental groups, housing charities and the Climate Change Committee, which warned it would delay the UK's net zero trajectory and lead to higher energy bills for renters in the long term.

Following the July 2024 general election, the Labour Government reinstated the EPC C ambition with revised targets: 2028 for new tenancies, 2030 for all tenancies — with a confirmed spending cap of £10,000.

milestones.title: £3,500 MEES Cost Cap — To Be Replaced by £10,000 Cap
milestones.summary: The existing £3,500 net cost cap (above which landlords can register a cost cap exemption from MEES) was set in 2015. The Government's May 2026 response confirmed this will be replaced by a £10,000 cap for the EPC C requirement, with a 10-year exemption validity period.
milestones.detail:
The £3,500 cost cap has been criticised as too low to cover the works required to bring many properties up to EPC E — let alone the forthcoming EPC C standard. In real terms, the cap has fallen significantly since 2015 due to building cost inflation.

The Government's May 2026 response to the PRS MEES consultation confirmed the replacement cap at £10,000 per property for the EPC C requirement (replacing an earlier consultation proposal of £15,000). Key features of the new cap:
• Applies to required energy efficiency improvements to achieve EPC C
• Landlords may register a 10-year exemption (extended from 5 years) if the standard cannot be achieved within the £10,000 cap
• The existing £3,500 cap remains in force for the current EPC E standard until the new regulations take effect
• Third-party funding (e.g. Warm Homes: Local Grant, ECO5, heat pump grants) can be counted against the cap

The final cap level was set lower than many landlord groups lobbied for (NRLA and ARLA Propertymark had advocated for £15,000–£25,000), but higher than the status quo. Until the new SI comes into force (expected 2027), the existing £3,500 cap applies to EPC E compliance.
milestones.source: MHCLG: Improving the Energy Performance of Privately Rented Homes — Government Response (May 2026)
